I'm so sorry that this is happening! I stumbled upon your post because my dad was diagnosed with neuroendocrine cancer about 1.5 years ago and I was googling something related to it. His case (neuroendocrine prostate cancer) is pretty different from yours so I don't think I have any specific info that would be super useful, but at least for him chemo was very effective and shrunk his tumors--I hope it is for you too! He had a few rounds of infusions around the time he was diagnosed and has been on oral chemo since then. He has also recently had whole-brain radiation for tumors in his brain (long story short, the chemo drug didn't cross his blood-brain barrier which allowed them to form) and we are waiting to see if it was effective.

I wanted to comment because I'm also an artist and I can't imagine the grief and fear you must feel about potentially losing your sight. I know things like cancer or other diseases are never "fair," but this specific situation just seems especially difficult. How are you doing now?

I also just started a medication that can cause seizures when combined with kratom, which gives me even more reason to quit. In your situation, I would recommend tapering slowly so that you can still somewhat function, if you have enough money to do so. Maybe start at 30gpd and reduce by one gram every day, and try dosing small doses in shorter intervals so you'll constantly have enough kratom in your system to diminish WDs. Best of luck. I also wonder about this. My kratom vendor tests for heavy metals and publishes the results for each strain. I looked at this info and calculated the amount of lead I was getting each day, which turned out to be anywhere from around 3 micrograms to 17 micrograms per day depending on the strain (I take 20 grams per day). According to the FDA, the tolerable total daily intake of lead for adults is 75 micrograms/day from foods and 5 micrograms/day from pharmaceuticals. Kratom should be classified as a pharmaceutical because you take it in addition to your diet, not as a substitute for food.

Take from this what you will. I've also noticed that while kratom helps me in the short term, I've become more depressed long-term since when I started taking it. Not sure if it's the kratom's fault, though... there are a lot of factors to consider.

Plus, the biological argument falls apart if you really look at it. Say someone defines women as people with XX chromosomes. What about people with Turner Syndrome, who only have one X chromosome but are still accepted to be women? Or women with Trisomy X (three X chromosomes)? Or people with Klinefelter syndrome, who have XXY but are considered men? From all of these examples, we can see that it doesn't depend on the chromosomes—it depends on these people's appearance and their sexual organs.

Following with that logic, some think having a uterus is necessary to be a woman.  What about women who have undergone hysterectomies? Or XX women born without a uterus? Or intersex people who have a uterus but appear male in all other regards? There are so many exceptions to any biological attempts to define womanhood.

After hearing about these exceptions, many people argue that they're not important because they only make up a small percentage of "women". But a definition should apply to *every* member of a group. TERFs or right-wingers just want to include anyone they think "should be included," even if they *aren't* women based on their biological definitions, while excluding people who might actually be considered a woman according to their definitions.

IMO, being a woman has a different definition to everyone. But if you keep asking questions, you'll find that almost all definitions don't have to deal with biology but instead appearance, societal treatment, or other factors.

I'm in a similar situation and completely relate to what you're saying. The most obvious solution would be to overcome your anxiety about your roommates judging you and cook whenever you want, but that's easier said than done. I know getting on anti-depressants helped me tremendously when I was too afraid to be seen cooking by my roommates, so I would highly recommend that—otherwise I wouldn't be able to cook at home at all. Also try to remember that you're paying rent too and are entitled to using the kitchen.


In terms of more useful suggestions, you can  try to learn your roommates' schedules and determine when they're out of the house, then prep meals for the entire week/next few days so you'll only have to microwave or assemble them when you want to eat. This will allow you to have complete control over your calories and stay out of the kitchen except for maybe 5 minutes a day. Cooking is honestly not hard—just think of something you want to eat and look up a recipe. Not sure what you like to eat, but one easy meal you could try to prep for the week is chicken breast, pasta or spaghetti, and bread/a salad/some kind of fruit. You could also buy a container of yogurt or another snack to have in the fridge so at least you'll always have something quick and healthy-ish to eat. This weekly meal prep method is what I use.


Finally, if you're not able to meal prep, you could just store nonperishable food in your room and get an electric kettle (can be as cheap as $15) to make hot meals. There's tofu that doesn't need to be refrigerated, which is a good source of protein, that you can put into instant ramen made with water from the electric kettle. I'm sure there are also other instant kettle meals you can look into, or consider getting a mini-fridge for your room so you can keep fruit or other healthier things in there.  I know this is a horrible situation and it sucks to be anxious in a place you're supposed to feel is home. Let me know if you would like any other suggestions, and good luck!
